This is a loaded question as-is. Do you refer to the First Cause argument? Or do you refer to "It's turtles all the way down!"?

The only capacity with which one can propose infinite regress of causation is by induction. Infinite regression is itself therefore not a fallacy if we arrive, by rational induction, to suppose "All things of set Ө observed behave thus, therefore all of set Ө may behave thus". Yet this is true only in the simple sense of what a fallacious argument is. What if, as taken true, it results in fallacious results as an axiom? That is, "fallacious by consequence"?

We cannot, however, say "All things of set Ө behave thus, therefore set β behaves thus". For Theta and Beta sets, even if they share similar elements, cannot be shown to be related in both having the same nature until all shared elements are discovered. Only inductively so. We can only suggest it as a possibility, based on shared elements, that other shared elements might occur.

From this we can easily see that, at best, an argument of infinite regression requires an argument of probability to be logical. Yet it's a very weak argument of probability, because not all things of set Ө are observed. Meaning the induction argument is limited only to observations made within the set "so far".

As Ө relates to our universe, empirical evidence does not support infinite regress of causation, for not all things have an observable cause. Which is effectively the same as saying they have no cause, for that which cannot be observed cannot be known to exist.

This solution requires we answer two additional question. "Can it be observed?" and "Can something exist with no observable effects?". If it has no effect it is not a cause, and if it cannot be observed it has no effect. For all things with effects can be observed by the effects they produce. If this is not true, we cannot prove the negative case, for we could not observe it (resulting in a circular logic fallacy).

Therefore, from that deduction on observations and effects, we can conclude that infinite regress is empirically unlikely if we observe a given phenomena to have no discoverable cause (that nothing can be observed as its cause).

Ideally, this is sufficient to answer the question with "It is deductively fallacious, and inductively improbable". We might further conclude the induction is fallacious, for it requires deductive answers to be circular (the unobservable phenomenon) as a consequence. Therefore we have no real reason or evidence to suppose infinite regression of causation exists. Or fallacious by consequence.

ITT we talk about our favorite GSGs. Be in depth, you get the drill

(or don't really it's cool either way)

Darkest Hour: A Hearts of Iron game - 2146 hours

This started as a mod/expansion thing for Hearts of Iron 2, and has been continually updated since it's release. While I personally wished it went into more detail, I really like the balance between diplomacy and warfare, the the event system is fairly well implemented.

Buuuuut that's not why anyone plays Darkest Hour. DH has, in my experience, the most kickass mods of any Paradox Plaza game. Fatherland, Fallout Doomsday, Hegemonia, New World Order 2, The Bonaparte Legacy, World in Conflict, and of course, the legendary Kaiserreich: Legacy of the Weltkrieg. That's not even mentioning any of the enhancement mods, my favorite of which being the Mixed Mod. Sadly, the update from 1.03 to 1.04 broke a lot of mods, and many of them were all but abandoned. A few guys on the forums are working to update the more popular ones, but many are still lost. You can always downgrade though, which is fantastic.

Victoria II - 647 hours

Compared to most other Paradox games, this one is short. Only 100 years to work with isn't much. What's more, the rebels are a total joke, the economy is sloppy at best, the army gameplay is even more of a joke, and the internal politics are... simple. But goddamnit, they nailed the diplomacy. 100% nailed it. If East vs. West had come out and been just like this I wouldn't complain one bit. The Spheres in Influence, the crises, the various agreements you can make and the AI just seem right to me. I'd have so many more hours in it if it wasn't so terrible on my PC.

Civilization 5 - 424 hours

pretty obvious one, yeah. That said, this game is pretty sick. The mechanics are easy to understand, the graphics are nice, it's just a nice, simple game to sit down to and play to relax for me. Plus, the mods are pretty great. Nothing like Darkest Hour's alt-history glory, but it's fun that Princess Celestia can call her loyal ally Adolf Hitler into her war against GabeN, Vladimir Lenin and Pagan Min.
